title: Une invitation aux Césars  (An Invitation to the Césars)

segments.t: Mathias, one of the agents, has been trying to arrange film work for Camille, an assistant at the agency. She is secretly his daughter. Now her colleagues Noemie and Herve notice an invitation to the Cesars on her desk. Assistants usually miss out on these French film awards. Listen to Camille try to explain her lucky invitation.
Une invitation aux Césars!
Moi, je n'ai pas eu d'invitation.
Moi non plus.
Les assistantes ne sont pas invitées. C'est quoi cette histoire?
C'est quoi cette invitation? Elle vient de qui?
Euh, je ne sais pas.
Non, je sais ce que c'est!
C'est à cause de l'autre soir avec Andréa.
J'ai travaillé très tard.
Et j'ai réparé son chemisier préféré.
Alors elle a voulu me remercier.
Et je lui ai donné une recette de pistou.
Ça doit être pour ça.
Je te déteste.
Let's go back to the envelope. Camille discovers the invitation, and her colleagues want to know why she has one.
Une invitation aux Césars!
'An invitation to the Cesars!' Camille reads the card she has just opened. The word before the awards combines 'to' and the plural word for 'the'. It names the event she is invited to.
Moi, je n'ai pas eu d'invitation.

'I didn't get an invitation.' Here's our language point: the everyday past, a helper word plus a past form. With a negative, the two little 'not' words wrap around the helper word only. Noémie joins in.
Moi non plus.
'Me neither.' Literally 'me not more'. It's the way to agree with a negative sentence. Then Noémie gets suspicious.
Les assistantes ne sont pas invitées.
'Assistants don't get invited.' The written words for 'assistants' and 'invited' both have feminine plural endings. Herve uses that form while including himself in the complaint.
C'est quoi cette histoire?
'What's going on?' Literally 'it's what, this story?'. A very common, slightly suspicious question. Hervé wants details.
C'est quoi cette invitation? Elle vient de qui?
'What's this invitation? Who's it from?' This second question ends on the question word, 'from who?', which is very relaxed and spoken. Camille is caught off guard.
Euh, je ne sais pas.
'Er, I don't know.' The first sound is French for 'um' or 'er'. Then an idea comes to her.
Non, je sais ce que c'est!
'No, I know what it is!' Notice the same verb, 'to know', in the negative a second ago and now in the positive. She starts inventing a story.
C'est à cause de l'autre soir avec Andréa.
'It's because of the other night with Andréa.' The words for 'because of' are worth learning as a block. And the details pile up.
J'ai travaillé très tard.
'I worked very late.' The everyday past again: 'have' plus 'worked'.
Et j'ai réparé son chemisier préféré.
'And I fixed her favourite blouse.' The same past pattern with the verb 'to repair'. She's getting into her stride.
Alors elle a voulu me remercier.
'So she wanted to thank me.' The first word, meaning 'so', links the cause and the result. Then she adds one more thing.
Et je lui ai donné une recette de pistou.
'And I gave her a recipe for pistou.' Pistou is a basil sauce from the south of France, where Camille comes from. A nice touch, and completely made up. She wraps it up.
Ça doit être pour ça.
'It must be for that.' The verb 'must' here shows a guess, the same way it does in English. Hervé has heard enough.
Je te déteste.

'I hate you.' In this context the strong words express a colleague's exaggerated jealousy. The small word before the action identifies the person being addressed. Now the whole scene once more. Now let's listen to the entire dialogue once more.
Une invitation aux Césars!
Moi, je n'ai pas eu d'invitation.
Moi non plus.
Les assistantes ne sont pas invitées. C'est quoi cette histoire?
C'est quoi cette invitation? Elle vient de qui?
Euh, je ne sais pas.
Non, je sais ce que c'est!
C'est à cause de l'autre soir avec Andréa.
J'ai travaillé très tard.
Et j'ai réparé son chemisier préféré.
Alors elle a voulu me remercier.
Et je lui ai donné une recette de pistou.
Ça doit être pour ça.
Je te déteste.
Camille has a ticket to the Césars, and two very jealous colleagues. If you heard the helper verb with the past forms, you've learned something you'll use every day. See you next time!
À bientôt!
